custom Web Component during its initialization (for example, inside `connectedCallback`), the following error is thrown:\\n\\n\\u003e Error: Assertion failed - heap is currently locked\\n\\u003eat mr (blazor.web.js:1:158963)\\n\\u003eat Object.beginInvokeDotNetFromJS\\n\\nThis happens in a Blazor WebAssembly project.The same approach works fine in a .NET MAUI Blazor Hybrid app.\\n\\nI'm aware that calling .NET from JS during component initialization isn't considered a good practice, but invoking .NET methods would help a gradual migration of a legacy web app to Blazor and MAUI. The goal is to integrate Blazor as a backend facade while preserving the existing UI for now, enabling the team to write new code in Blazor moving forward.\\nThe documentation does not appear to impose any restriction that prevents from using this to handle JS calls:  [Link to docs.](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/blazor/javascript-interoperability/call-dotnet-from-javascript?view=aspnetcore-9.0#invoke-a-static-net-method)\\n\\n## Minimal repro repo\\n[https://github.com/alexuaua/BlazorDotNetInteropDemo](https://github.com/alexuaua/BlazorDotNetInteropDemo)\\n\\n## Steps to reproduce\\n1. Clone the repo.\\n2. Run the project and switch to the Counter page.\\n3. Open the browser console.\\n4. Observe the `heap is currently locked` error (only) during initialization  of the web component.\\n\\n## Expected behaviour\\nThe JS-to-.NET interop call should succeed (as it does in MAUI Blazor), or there should be a documented workaround for such use cases. Alternatively, the documentation should clearly explain the restrictions on using DotNet.invokeMethodAsync in Blazor WebAssembly apps.\\n\\n## Actual behaviour\\nThe interop call fails due to what appears to be a race condition.\\n\\nDeferring the call using `setTimeout` (i.e. placing the call later in the stack) resolves the issue, this workaround is even shown in community resources like [Blazor University](https://blazor-university.com/javascript-interop/calling-dotnet-from-javascript/calling-static-dotnet-methods/). \\n\\nThat said, it would be **very helpful if**:\\n- The official documentation explicitly described this race condition and recommended patterns for `DotNet.invokeMethodAsync` in component scenarios.\\n- Blazor could provide a way to queue interop calls that are attempted during initialization - would be helpful for migration projects where modifying component logic is non-trivial.\\nUnless I’m missing something, the tasks performed in the demo do not require synchronous execution. Blazor WebAssembly’s rendering engine is based on its own component lifecycle and does not track or wait for hydration of external DOM elements, such as those created by Web Components.\\n\\nThis issue blocks a real-world migration scenario where we cannot immediately rewrite all UI in Blazor. Summary\\r\\nMark the `IApplicationBuilder.UseWebAssemblyDebugging()` extension (in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server`) as obsolete and stop emitting it from our project templates. Modern IDEs (Visual Studio, VS Code) launch the debug proxy directly. This does mean that the legacy in-browser (Ctrl+Alt+D) will no longer be supported.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Background\\r\\n- `UseWebAssemblyDebugging()` is defined in `src/Components/WebAssembly/Server/src/WebAssemblyNetDebugProxyAppBuilderExtensions.cs`. It maps `/_framework/debug` and uses `DebugProxyLauncher` to start the browser debug proxy (`BlazorDebugProxy/BrowserDebugHost.dll`) for the legacy Chromium/Firefox in-browser experience.\\r\\n- Related configuration that only exists to support this path:\\r\\n  - The `inspectUri` value in `launchSettings.json` (`.../_framework/debug/ws-proxy?browser={browserInspectUri}`). This is present in test assets but **not** in the shipping templates.\\r\\n  - `NO_PROXY` handling and the `/_framework/debug` endpoint, both internal to the middleware/launcher.\\r\\n- The IDE-driven debugger launches the debug proxy directly and does not depend on this middleware.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Customer impact\\r\\nUsage of the legacy in-browser debugging path appears low. The strongest signal is #61559 (Apr 2025), where browser debugging was broken out of the box on recent Chromium versions for roughly a month; it drew only 11 distinct commenters and no upvotes, and overall issue volume for this path is very small. We may still receive some complaints from users who rely on browser-only debugging (e.g. without Visual Studio, or in Firefox), so we should be sensitive to that in messaging.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Proposed changes\\r\\n1. **Obsolete the API** — Add `[Obsolete]` to `WebAssemblyNetDebugProxyAppBuilderExtensions.UseWebAssemblyDebugging`, using the next diagnostic ID (`ASPDEPR011`) and a new `AspNetCoreDeprecate011Url` entry in `src/Shared/Obsoletions.cs`. Update the public API baseline files (`PublicAPI.Shipped.txt` / `PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt`).\\r\\n\\r\\n   Obsoletion message:\\r\\n   \\u003e `\\\"UseWebAssemblyDebugging is obsolete and should be removed along with any inspectUri configurations. Blazor WebAssembly debugging is now launched directly by Visual Studio and Visual Studio Code.\\\"`\\r\\n\\r\\n2. **Remove from the Blazor Web App template** — Remove `app.UseWebAssemblyDebugging();` (guarded by `#if (UseWebAssembly)`) from:\\r\\n   - `src/ProjectTemplates/Web.ProjectTemplates/content/BlazorWeb-CSharp/BlazorWebCSharp.1/Program.cs`\\r\\n   - `src/ProjectTemplates/Web.ProjectTemplates/content/BlazorWeb-CSharp/BlazorWebCSharp.1/Program.Main.cs`\\r\\n\\r\\n   Collapse the now-redundant `#if (UseWebAssembly || IndividualLocalAuth)` / `#if (UseWebAssembly)` conditionals accordingly, and update template baseline/snapshot tests.\\r\\n\\r\\n3. **Standalone Blazor WebAssembly template** — Verified no change needed: `ComponentsWebAssembly-CSharp` is client-only and does not reference `UseWebAssemblyDebugging` or `inspectUri`.\\r\\n\\r\\n4. **Resolve the internal caller** — `src/Components/WebAssembly/DevServer/src/Server/Startup.cs` calls `UseWebAssemblyDebugging()`. Suppress the new obsoletion warning there (with a justifying comment) so the repo continues to build.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Related work\\r\\n- Companion issue: Deprecate the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.DevServer` package — contact:** @javiercn\n\n## Scenario\n\n**This scenario validates that a fix works.** A native app hosting Blazor is closed, backgrounded and navigated around far more abruptly than a web page, and its components are often in the middle of talking to JavaScript when that happens. Disposing an `IJSObjectReference` after the WebView had gone threw `JSDisconnectedException`, which showed up as hangs on teardown and alarming errors in the debug output. Navigation and disposal now mark the JS runtime disconnected before components are disposed, and that exception is caught and discarded.\n\nThis validates that a Hybrid app tears down cleanly.\n\n## Minimum build\n\n.NET 11 Preview 7 or later.\n\n## Configurations to cover\n\n* Blazor Web App\n  * [ ] Static SSR\n  * [ ] Interactive Server\n  * [ ] Interactive WebAssembly\n  * [ ] Interactive Auto\n* [ ] Standalone WebAssembly\n* [x] Hybrid (MAUI)\n\n## Also exercise\n\n* [ ] Published output\n* [ ] An existing .NET 10 app upgraded to .NET 11\n* [ ] Trimming or ahead-of-time compilation\n* [ ] More than one server instance, or a proxy in front\n* [ ] Hot Reload\n* [ ] An IDE as well as the command line\n* [ ] Container\n\n## Setup\n\nYou need the workloads for building a native app for at least one platform, and a device or emulator. Covering more than one platform is worthwhile, since the embedded browser differs between them.\n\n## What to build\n\nA native app hosting Blazor, with pages that are busy in ways that make teardown awkward. Include a page that keeps a JavaScript module loaded and calls into it repeatedly, one that starts a slow JavaScript call and does not wait for it, one with a timer that keeps firing, and one that has registered .NET methods for JavaScript to call back into. Give the components proper cleanup so you can tell whether it runs. Add a native page alongside the Blazor content so you can move between the two kinds of screen, and log to the debug output when each component is cleaned up.\n\n## Things to try\n\n* Navigating away from each busy page while it is mid-flight.\n* Moving from a Blazor screen to a native screen and back, repeatedly.\n* Closing the app while a page is in the middle of a JavaScript call.\n* Backgrounding the app and returning to it, and backgrounding it and then closing it.\n* Using the operating system's back gesture or button rather than in-app navigation.\n* Rotating the device while a page is busy.\n* Repeating the cycle many times in one session and watching memory.\n* Watching the debug output throughout for exceptions and warnings.\n\n## Expected behavior\n\nTeardown completes promptly however busy the page was, and calls that were already in flight go quietly.\n\n### Must hold\n\n* Leaving each busy page runs its cleanup and does not hang.\n* Closing the app while a JavaScript call is in flight terminates promptly rather than waiting on work that will never finish.\n* No exception from calls that were in flight appears in the debug output. In particular, disposing a JavaScript object reference after the connection is gone must not surface a `JSDisconnectedException`.\n* Repeated moves between Blazor and native screens leave memory stable across the session.\n* Returning from the background finds the app in a working state.\n\n### Expected differences between configurations\n\n* The embedded browser differs between platforms, so cover more than one if you can. A teardown that is clean on one platform and not on another is a finding.\n\n## Documentation to use\n\n* [ASP.NET Core Blazor Hybrid](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/blazor/hybrid/?view=aspnetcore-11.0)\n* [Component disposal](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/blazor/components/component-disposal?view=aspnetcore-11.0)\n\n## What to report\n\nReport results using the format described in the [validation testing manual](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/68479). will be a while before we get to this, but various parts of the architecture are already designed with this in mind.\r\n\r\nWe should support running Blazor in two modes, auto-selecting which one is best for the current user's browser:\r\n\r\n * **On the browser's main JS thread**, which is necessary for older browsers that don't support WebWorker. The .NET/JS interop can continue using shared memory if we find it's necessary to have good perf on those older browsers (and thread safety is not difficult because it's all synchronous).\r\n * **In a web worker (background thread) on more up-to-date browsers**. The .NET/JS interop will need to work by serializing any data that is being transferred rather than passing pointers [1].\r\n\r\nThis will be advantageous because then, even if your .NET code does something that locks up the CPU (such as a GC cycle), the UI will remain perfectly smooth (e.g., during animations or scrolling, or while the user is typing quickly into a textbox).\r\n\r\nThe existing UI update mechanism is designed around transferring batches of minimal diffs from .NET to JS, so it shouldn't be hugely difficult to have it express those diffs as serialized data rather than pointers into the WASM memory space. We'll have to be careful around things like event handling to ensure that the asynchrony can't result in inconsistency of behaviour versus the synchronous single-threaded model. For example, we will need to force all event delivery to be async as far as the JS side is concerned, even in the non-worker-thread case.\r\n\r\n*[1] Strictly speaking, we could also do it with shared memory on even newer browsers that support SharedArrayBuffer. But if we can get satisfactory perf without this, it would be better to serialize because it would mean fewer combinations of browser scenarios, and saves us having to deal with potentially complex thread-safety concerns on the .NET .NET trimmer statically analyzes your project and removes any unused code. In Blazor we use the .NET trimmer to significantly reduce the publish size of Blazor WebAssembly apps. However, we don't currently use the .NET trimmer to its fullest potential. We currently configure the trimmer in a partial mode, which only trims assemblies that are explicitly marked as trimmable. This typically means that the app assembly itself and many dependencies are not trimmed. This is a conservative setting that optimizes for maintaining functionality over reducing app size. \r\n\r\nThe default trim mode for the .NET trimmer is to trim everything. This is the mode used by the .NET Native AOT workloads.Analyzers provide warnings if there are code paths in the app that are not safe to trim. Given how sensitive web apps are to download size and load time, it seems like doing full trimming should be the goal for Blazor.\r\n\r\nEnabling support for full trimming also is a potential solution to enabling a [single project model for Blazor Web Apps](#49079) that target both server and browser. When you multitarget a project, everything in the project is built for both targets unless you indicated otherwise. This is problematic for browser scenarios because you may potentially bring in dependencies, components, and code into the browser targeted build that are only needed on the server. However, if we could enable full trimming *and* indicate to the trimmer which components are setup to render on WebAssembly, then the browser build could be aggressively trimmed to remove any unwanted code and dependencies.\r\n\r\nEnabling support for full .NET trimming typically means removing any dynamic code path that are based on reflection. We would need to make Blazor apps trimmer friendly by removing this code using techniques like source generators. For example, in Blazor we use reflection as part of the component discovery process and in the render tree builder code generated by the Razor compiler. We're already working on enabling [component discovery through source generation](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/48767). We also have on our backlog to [handle component parameters through source generation](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/29550). There may be other related work items as well.\r\n\r\nThere is also ecosystem impact of enabling full trimming by default. Many .NET libraries are not setup for trimming and would potentially need to be updated. It will take some time to work through these issues with the Blazor community. Certain features also simply wouldn't work with full trimming. For example, dynamically loading dependencies at runtime that are not known statically. For backwards compatibility, app developers can configure the trimmer to not trim assemblies that are not yet trimmer friendly. We'd need to understand better all the cases that get impacted by full trimming and ensure we provide a reasonable user experience for addressing by @SteveSandersonMS] This issue was originally reported by @verdie-g as follows below the line. On investigation the problem is that C# has added a new syntax that doesn't work in Razor.**\r\n\r\nThe Razor compiler allows arbitrary C# code within `@{ ... }` blocks. Unfortunately this means it allows the use of local functions in a way that confuses the parsing logic, causing it to use the wrong `__builder` instance. Example:\r\n\r\n```razor\r\n\u003cFluentTreeView\u003e\r\n@{\r\n    RenderTree(0, 3);\r\n\r\n    void RenderTree(int depth, int maxDepth)\r\n    {\r\n        if (depth \u003e= maxDepth)\r\n        {\r\n            return;\r\n        }\r\n\r\n        \u003cFluentTreeItem Text=\"item\"\u003e\r\n            @{ RenderTree(depth + 1, maxDepth); }\r\n        \u003c/FluentTreeItem\u003e\r\n    }\r\n}\r\n\u003c/FluentTreeView\u003e\r\n```\r\n\r\nHere, the child content of `FluentTreeItem` should be compiled as a `RenderFragment` that acts on whatever `RenderTreeBuilder` is passed in. But because of C# scoping rules, the `RenderFragment` actually acts on the `__builder` captured from its parent context, so it is simply corrupting the output instead of doing something useful.\r\n\r\nPossible solutions:\r\n\r\n1. We could ask for the Razor compiler block the use of local functions inside `@{ ... }` specifically. However that's probably impractical because Razor doesn't parse the contents of `@{ ... }`.\r\n   * Perhaps it is achievable as an analyzer that acts on the code *after* the Razor compiler has generated it.\r\n2. We could do something in the runtime to detect more generally any cases where the wrong `RenderTreeBuilder` is invoked. For example if the runtime set an \"rendering in progress\" flag on it before it starts rendering and synchronously unsets that flag at the end of rendering, then it would have caught this case because child components are rendered afterwards (not recursively), so when the child is rendered it would see it's trying to write to a builder that does not have the \"rendering in progress\" flag set.\r\n   * Drawback: how do we even check if this flag is set? We would **not** check it as part of each rendering instruction. There's plenty of evidence that rendering perf is sensitive to that kind of thing (and we can't just check it in development either).\r\n   * Possible solution: instead of just setting a flag, actually null out the referencing to the underlying buffer (storing it in some other field to be swapped back later). Then if anyone tries to write to the builder while it's not marked as rendering-in-progress, they will get a `NullReferenceException` instead of corrupt output. Obviously that's not super easy to understand but avoids any perf cost.\r\n\r\n---------\r\n\r\n### Is there an existing issue for this?\r\n\r\n- [X] I have searched the existing issues\r\n\r\n### Web Component during its initialization (for example, inside `connectedCallback`), the following error is thrown:\n\n\u003e Error: Assertion failed - heap is currently locked\n\u003eat mr (blazor.web.js:1:158963)\n\u003eat Object.beginInvokeDotNetFromJS\n\nThis happens in a Blazor WebAssembly project.The same approach works fine in a .NET MAUI Blazor Hybrid app.\n\nI'm aware that calling .NET from JS during component initialization isn't considered a good practice, but invoking .NET methods would help a gradual migration of a legacy web app to Blazor and MAUI. The goal is to integrate Blazor as a backend facade while preserving the existing UI for now, enabling the team to write new code in Blazor moving forward.\nThe documentation does not appear to impose any restriction that prevents from using this to handle JS calls:  [Link to docs.](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/blazor/javascript-interoperability/call-dotnet-from-javascript?view=aspnetcore-9.0#invoke-a-static-net-method)\n\n## Minimal repro repo\n[https://github.com/alexuaua/BlazorDotNetInteropDemo](https://github.com/alexuaua/BlazorDotNetInteropDemo)\n\n## Steps to reproduce\n1. Clone the repo.\n2. Run the project and switch to the Counter page.\n3. Open the browser console.\n4. Observe the `heap is currently locked` error (only) during initialization  of the web component.\n\n## Expected behaviour\nThe JS-to-.NET interop call should succeed (as it does in MAUI Blazor), or there should be a documented workaround for such use cases. Alternatively, the documentation should clearly explain the restrictions on using DotNet.invokeMethodAsync in Blazor WebAssembly apps.\n\n## Actual behaviour\nThe interop call fails due to what appears to be a race condition.\n\nDeferring the call using `setTimeout` (i.e. placing the call later in the stack) resolves the issue, this workaround is even shown in community resources like [Blazor University](https://blazor-university.com/javascript-interop/calling-dotnet-from-javascript/calling-static-dotnet-methods/). \n\nThat said, it would be **very helpful if**:\n- The official documentation explicitly described this race condition and recommended patterns for `DotNet.invokeMethodAsync` in component scenarios.\n- Blazor could provide a way to queue interop calls that are attempted during initialization - would be helpful for migration projects where modifying component logic is non-trivial.\nUnless I’m missing something, the tasks performed in the demo do not require synchronous execution. Blazor WebAssembly’s rendering engine is based on its own component lifecycle and does not track or wait for hydration of external DOM elements, such as those created by Web Components.\n\nThis issue blocks a real-world migration scenario where we cannot immediately rewrite all UI in Blazor. Summary\r\nMark the `IApplicationBuilder.UseWebAssemblyDebugging()` extension (in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server`) as obsolete and stop emitting it from our project templates. Modern IDEs (Visual Studio, VS Code) launch the debug proxy directly. This does mean that the legacy in-browser (Ctrl+Alt+D) will no longer be supported.\r\n\r\n## Background\r\n- `UseWebAssemblyDebugging()` is defined in `src/Components/WebAssembly/Server/src/WebAssemblyNetDebugProxyAppBuilderExtensions.cs`. It maps `/_framework/debug` and uses `DebugProxyLauncher` to start the browser debug proxy (`BlazorDebugProxy/BrowserDebugHost.dll`) for the legacy Chromium/Firefox in-browser experience.\r\n- Related configuration that only exists to support this path:\r\n  - The `inspectUri` value in `launchSettings.json` (`.../_framework/debug/ws-proxy?browser={browserInspectUri}`). This is present in test assets but **not** in the shipping templates.\r\n  - `NO_PROXY` handling and the `/_framework/debug` endpoint, both internal to the middleware/launcher.\r\n- The IDE-driven debugger launches the debug proxy directly and does not depend on this middleware.\r\n\r\n## Customer impact\r\nUsage of the legacy in-browser debugging path appears low. The strongest signal is #61559 (Apr 2025), where browser debugging was broken out of the box on recent Chromium versions for roughly a month; it drew only 11 distinct commenters and no upvotes, and overall issue volume for this path is very small. We may still receive some complaints from users who rely on browser-only debugging (e.g. without Visual Studio, or in Firefox), so we should be sensitive to that in messaging.\r\n\r\n## Proposed changes\r\n1. **Obsolete the API** — Add `[Obsolete]` to `WebAssemblyNetDebugProxyAppBuilderExtensions.UseWebAssemblyDebugging`, using the next diagnostic ID (`ASPDEPR011`) and a new `AspNetCoreDeprecate011Url` entry in `src/Shared/Obsoletions.cs`. Update the public API baseline files (`PublicAPI.Shipped.txt` / `PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt`).\r\n\r\n   Obsoletion message:\r\n   \u003e `\"UseWebAssemblyDebugging is obsolete and should be removed along with any inspectUri configurations. Blazor WebAssembly debugging is now launched directly by Visual Studio and Visual Studio Code.\"`\r\n\r\n2. **Remove from the Blazor Web App template** — Remove `app.UseWebAssemblyDebugging();` (guarded by `#if (UseWebAssembly)`) from:\r\n   - `src/ProjectTemplates/Web.ProjectTemplates/content/BlazorWeb-CSharp/BlazorWebCSharp.1/Program.cs`\r\n   - `src/ProjectTemplates/Web.ProjectTemplates/content/BlazorWeb-CSharp/BlazorWebCSharp.1/Program.Main.cs`\r\n\r\n   Collapse the now-redundant `#if (UseWebAssembly || IndividualLocalAuth)` / `#if (UseWebAssembly)` conditionals accordingly, and update template baseline/snapshot tests.\r\n\r\n3. **Standalone Blazor WebAssembly template** — Verified no change needed: `ComponentsWebAssembly-CSharp` is client-only and does not reference `UseWebAssemblyDebugging` or `inspectUri`.\r\n\r\n4. **Resolve the internal caller** — `src/Components/WebAssembly/DevServer/src/Server/Startup.cs` calls `UseWebAssemblyDebugging()`. Suppress the new obsoletion warning there (with a justifying comment) so the repo continues to build.\r\n\r\n## Related work\r\n- Companion issue: Deprecate the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.DevServer` package — Description\\r\\n\\r\\nThese set of APIs allow Blazor, MVC and Razor pages to map well-known URLs to content-specific (fingerprinted URLs).\\r\\n\\r\\n## Scenarios\\r\\n\\r\\n### Startup/Program APIs\\r\\n\\r\\nThe list of assets is defined on a per-endpoint basis. MVC and RazorPages opt-in to the feature via a call to `WithResourceCollection` following the call to `MapRazorPages()` or `MapControllers()`.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis call adds a `ResourceAssetCollection` to the Metadata collection of the endpoints, which contains the mapping between human-readable URLs and content-specific URLs.\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom there, other components can retrieve the mapping from endpoint metadata.\\r\\n\\r\\n```diff\\r\\napp.MapStaticAssets();\\r\\n\\r\\napp.MapRazorPages()\\r\\n+   .WithResourceCollection();\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nSince we can have calls to map different manifests, `WithResourceCollection` takes a parameter to provide the Id for the matching `MatchStaticAssets`.\\r\\n\\r\\n```diff\\r\\napp.MapStaticAssets(\\\"WebassemblyApp1.Client\\\");\\r\\napp.MapStaticAssets(\\\"WebassemblyApp2.Client\\\");\\r\\n\\r\\napp.MapRazorPages()\\r\\n+   .WithResourceCollection(\\\"WebassemblyApp1.Client\\\");\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### Consuming the mapped assets\\r\\n\\r\\nThe assets are consumed indirectly from MVC and Razor Pages via existing `Script`, `Image`, `Link`, and `Url` tag helpers.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn Blazor, the assets are consumed via the `Assets` property in `ComponentBase` which exposes an indexer to resolve the fingerprinted url for a given asset.\\r\\n\\r\\n```html\\r\\n\\u003clink rel=\\\"stylesheet\\\" href=\\\"@Assets[\\\"app.css\\\"]\\\" /\\u003e\\r\\n\\u003clink rel=\\\"stylesheet\\\" href=\\\"@Assets[\\\"BlazorWeb-CSharp.styles.css\\\"]\\\" /\\u003e\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThis in the future will be cleaner with a compiler feature similar to the Url tag helper in MVC that transforms \\\"~/app.css\\\" into the above code inside the href attribute.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn addition to this, there are two built-in components to generate an importmap for scripts. See [here](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/script/type/importmap) for details.\\r\\n\\r\\n**TL;DR: Creates a mapping for calls to `import` and script `type=\\\"module\\\"` that optionally includes integrity information**. A sample:\\r\\n\\r\\n```html\\r\\n\\u003cscript type=\\\"importmap\\\"\\u003e\\r\\n  {\\r\\n    \\\"imports\\\": {\\r\\n      \\\"square\\\": \\\"./module/shapes/square.js\\\"\\r\\n    },\\r\\n }\\r\\n\\u003c/script\\u003e\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThere is an ImportMap blazor component\\r\\n```html\\r\\n\\u003cImportMap /\\u003e\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nand in MVC we extended the script tag helper to Is there an existing issue for this?\\n\\n- [x] I have searched the existing issues\\n\\n### Describe the bug\\n\\nAccording to the [documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/release-notes/aspnetcore-10.0?view=aspnetcore-10.0#client-side-fingerprinting), there appear to be two ways to enable client-side fingerprinting:\\n\\n1. Add the marker `#[.{fingerprint}]` to references so that non-framework static files are fingerprinted.\\n2. Use the `StaticWebAssetFingerprintPattern` attribute to control which assets get fingerprinted.\\n\\nHowever, when I run dotnet publish for a Blazor WebAssembly app, the generated index.html automatically includes fingerprint markers for JavaScript files under wwwroot that are not part of the Blazor framework. The problem is that the actual file names are not rewritten to include the fingerprint. As a result, when hosting the contents of publish/wwwroot, those script requests return 404 errors because the referenced (fingerprinted) logical names do not exist on disk.\\n\\n```\\nGET http://[::]:8000/lib/bootstrap/dist/js/bootstrap.bundle.min.493y06b0oq.js net::ERR_ABORTED 404 (File not found)\\nGET http://[::]:8000/lib/bootstrap/dist/js/bootstrap.29cdq58tmq.js net::ERR_ABORTED 404 (File not found)\\n```\\n\\n### Expected Behavior\\n\\nIf I do NOT configure any `StaticWebAssetFingerprintPattern`, non-framework JavaScript files should be referenced as-is (without fingerprint markers).\\nAlternatively, if fingerprinting markers are added, the process should be consistent (either rewrite file names accordingly or avoid adding markers).\\n\\nThis appears aligned with the workaround mentioned in this issue comment:\\nhttps://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/62211#issuecomment-3146544516\\n\\nIncluding the following in the project fixes the inconsistency:\\n\\n```xml\\n\\u003cStaticWebAssetFingerprintPattern Include=\\\"JS\\\" Pattern=\\\"*.js\\\" Expression=\\\"#[.{fingerprint}]!\\\" /\\u003e\\n```\\n\\nAdditionally, it is desirable for the template to work as is.\\n\\n### Steps To Reproduce\\n\\n1. Install .NET 10 RC2\\n2. Run: dotnet new blazorwasm -f net10.0\\n3. Run: dotnet publish\\n4. Host the published app, e.g.:\\n```\\ncd bin/Release/net10.0/publish/wwwroot\\npython3 -m http.server\\n```\\n5. Open the site in a browser and observe 404 errors for some JavaScript references.\\n\\n\\n### Exceptions (if any)\\n\\n_No response_\\n\\n### .NET Version\\n\\n10.0.100-rc.2.25502.107\\n\\n### appear, the application continues to function normally.\\n\\nThe root cause seems to be that `dotnet.js` is **not fingerprinted** during publish, so browsers aggressively cache an outdated version across deployments.\\n\\nThis mismatch does not immediately break the app, but could cause issues with larger version upgrades in the future.\\n\\n### Expected Behavior\\n\\nThere should be no version mismatch warnings in the browser console after publishing a new version.\\n\\nIdeally, `dotnet.js` should be fingerprinted (e.g., `/dotnet.[hash].js`) during publish, just like `dotnet.runtime.js` and `dotnet.native.js` are.\\n\\nThis would prevent caching issues and ensure version consistency.\\n\\n\\n### Steps To Reproduce\\n\\n1. Publish a new version of a Blazor WebAssembly Hosted app (e.g., upgrade from .NET 9.0.3 to 9.0.4).\\n2. Visit the site without clearing browser cache.\\n3. Open browser DevTools (F12) and check the console.\\n4. Observe mismatch warnings for dotnet.runtime.js and dotnet.native.js compared to dotnet.js.\\n\\n\\n### Exceptions (if any)\\n\\nNo unhandled exceptions.\\n\\nOnly console warnings are shown.\\nApplication still runs successfully.\\n\\n### .NET Version\\n\\n9.0.201\\n\\n### Anything else?\\n\\nSuggestion: Please fingerprint `dotnet.js` during publish, similar to other WebAssembly runtime assets.\\n\\nAlternatively, provide a built-in cache-busting mechanism for critical runtime files at startup.\\n\\nThis would avoid unnecessary confusion for developers and prevent potential Background\\r\\n\\r\\nUpon initialization, the `dotnet watch` tool needs to know the set of available WebAssembly hot reload capabilities before the hot reload session starts. The current mechanism for this relies on the WebAssembly runtime having started up so it can be asked which capabilities it supports. However, in Blazor Web scenarios, WebAssembly runtime startup might be delayed indefinitely, which causes the mechanism to read hot reload capabilities to fail.\\r\\n\\r\\nWe worked around this problem in https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/pull/36195 by having a fallback, default set of capabilities to use if reading capabilities from the WebAssembly runtime fails.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Proposed solution\\r\\nWe could go one of two directions in the future to fully address this issue:\\r\\n* Expand the capabilities of `dotnet watch` to dynamically update the set of available capabilities if a new runtime becomes available (relatively high complexity)\\r\\n* Remove WebAssembly capabilities detection completely and rely on the fallback capabilities only (simpler)\\r\\n\\r\\nTo simplify the Blazor WebAssembly hot reload infrastructure and make the overall hot reload experience less error prone, I propose we go with the 2nd option that simplifies WebAssembly hot reload capabilities detection by having the full set of capabilities be known by the `dotnet watch` tool without having to dynamically fetch those capabilities from the WebAssembly Is there an existing issue for this?\\r\\n\\r\\n- [X] I have searched the existing issues\\r\\n\\r\\n### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe the problem.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt's known issue that dotnet.wasm is a large file that every user of blazor browser should download. It's 44Mb for the project that I work on. Brotli compresses it to 9MB which is way better. However this compression comes at the cost that the client app needs to deal with the decompression by itself and needs brotly-dec-wasm library and each developer manually should mess around with the files and boot blazor.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Describe the solution you'd like\\r\\n\\r\\nIt'd be better if such job is done natively between server-browser. However there's a problem, that for instance, Azure CDN has a limit of 8MB for a file to be eligible for compressing. If it was possible to split dotnet.wasm during publishing to multiple chunks then this would problem resolved automatically on the browser level.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Additional context\\r\\n\\r\\nUPD 02.11.2023. Clarifying feature request a little bit here.\\r\\nThe way how Blazor publishes bundles does not play way with major CDN providers ([Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cdn/cdn-improve-performance#azure-cdn-standard-from-microsoft-profiles) and [AWS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/ServingCompressedFiles.html) and [GCP](https://cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/dynamic-compression#response-not-compressed)) because they have limit ~10Mb for the file to be compressed. Blazor produces files within the bundle (dotnet.wasm specifically) which are larger than that thus making developers implement their own DIY loader if they want both consume compressed bundle and use those CDN providers.\\r\\nOne of ways to overcome this is to give developers the control of the maximum size of an item in the bundle. E.g. in ``.csproj`` file like:\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\u003cMaxPublishItemSize\\u003e5Mb\\u003c/MaxPublishItemSize\\u003e\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe metadata about file chunks can be reflected in ``blazor.boot.json`` file and used by the loaded to download and merge the chunks Please describe the problem.\\n\\nYes, my feature request is related to optimizing frontend performance in ASP.NET Core applications. Currently, ASP.NET Core heavily relies on JavaScript for client-side operations, which can sometimes lead to performance bottlenecks, especially in complex web applications with intensive client-side processing. This reliance on JavaScript can limit the performance potential, particularly in scenarios requiring heavy computation or real-time data processing on the client side.\\n\\n### Describe the solution you'd like\\n\\nI propose the integration of WebAssembly (WASM) support within ASP.NET Core. This solution would involve:\\r\\n\\r\\nEnabling developers to write C# code that compiles to WebAssembly, allowing intensive computations to be run in the browser at near-native speeds.\\r\\nProviding seamless interoperability between WASM modules and existing JavaScript frameworks/libraries used in ASP.NET Core applications.\\r\\nOffering tools and documentation to assist developers in migrating performance-critical JavaScript code to C# (or another .NET language), which would then compile to WASM.\\r\\nEnsuring the WASM integration is aligned with the current development workflow in ASP.NET Core, allowing developers to adopt it incrementally in their existing projects.\\r\\nThe addition of WebAssembly support would significantly enhance the capabilities of ASP.NET Core for building high-performance, client-side web applications. It would also open up new possibilities for complex front-end development using the .NET stack, aligning ASP.NET Core with modern web development standards and performance expectations.\\n\\n### Description\r\n\r\nThese set of APIs allow Blazor, MVC and Razor pages to map well-known URLs to content-specific (fingerprinted URLs).\r\n\r\n## Scenarios\r\n\r\n### Startup/Program APIs\r\n\r\nThe list of assets is defined on a per-endpoint basis. MVC and RazorPages opt-in to the feature via a call to `WithResourceCollection` following the call to `MapRazorPages()` or `MapControllers()`.\r\n\r\nThis call adds a `ResourceAssetCollection` to the Metadata collection of the endpoints, which contains the mapping between human-readable URLs and content-specific URLs.\r\n\r\nFrom there, other components can retrieve the mapping from endpoint metadata.\r\n\r\n```diff\r\napp.MapStaticAssets();\r\n\r\napp.MapRazorPages()\r\n+   .WithResourceCollection();\r\n```\r\n\r\nSince we can have calls to map different manifests, `WithResourceCollection` takes a parameter to provide the Id for the matching `MatchStaticAssets`.\r\n\r\n```diff\r\napp.MapStaticAssets(\"WebassemblyApp1.Client\");\r\napp.MapStaticAssets(\"WebassemblyApp2.Client\");\r\n\r\napp.MapRazorPages()\r\n+   .WithResourceCollection(\"WebassemblyApp1.Client\");\r\n```\r\n\r\n### Consuming the mapped assets\r\n\r\nThe assets are consumed indirectly from MVC and Razor Pages via existing `Script`, `Image`, `Link`, and `Url` tag helpers.\r\n\r\nIn Blazor, the assets are consumed via the `Assets` property in `ComponentBase` which exposes an indexer to resolve the fingerprinted url for a given asset.\r\n\r\n```html\r\n\u003clink rel=\"stylesheet\" href=\"@Assets[\"app.css\"]\" /\u003e\r\n\u003clink rel=\"stylesheet\" href=\"@Assets[\"BlazorWeb-CSharp.styles.css\"]\" /\u003e\r\n```\r\n\r\nThis in the future will be cleaner with a compiler feature similar to the Url tag helper in MVC that transforms \"~/app.css\" into the above code inside the href attribute.\r\n\r\nIn addition to this, there are two built-in components to generate an importmap for scripts. See [here](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/script/type/importmap) for details.\r\n\r\n**TL;DR: Creates a mapping for calls to `import` and script `type=\"module\"` that optionally includes integrity information**. A sample:\r\n\r\n```html\r\n\u003cscript type=\"importmap\"\u003e\r\n  {\r\n    \"imports\": {\r\n      \"square\": \"./module/shapes/square.js\"\r\n    },\r\n    \"integrity\": {\r\n      \"./module/shapes/square.js\": \"sha384-oqVuAfXRKap7fdgcCY5uykM6+R9GqQ8K/uxy9rx7HNQlGYl1kPzQho1wx4JwY8wC\"\r\n    }\r\n  }\r\n\u003c/script\u003e\r\n```\r\n\r\nThere is an ImportMap blazor component\r\n```html\r\n\u003cImportMap /\u003e\r\n```\r\n\r\nand in MVC we extended the script tag helper to support it\r\n```html\r\n\u003cscript type=\"importmap\"\u003e\u003c/script\u003e\r\n```\r\n\r\n### Layering\r\n\r\nI included this section to explain the reasons for some of the APIs below.\r\n\r\n```mermaid\r\nflowchart LR\r\n    subgraph AspNet[ASP.NET Framework reference]\r\n        StaticAssets[Static Assets]\r\n        Endpoints[Components Endpoints SSR]\r\n        MVCRp[Mvc and Razor Pages]\r\n    end\r\n    Components[Components]\r\n    ComponentsWasm[Components Webassembly]\r\n    ComponentsWebView[Components WebView]\r\n    ComponentsWasm--\u003eComponents\r\n    ComponentsWebView--\u003eComponents\r\n    Endpoints--\u003eComponents\r\n    Endpoints--\u003eStaticAssets\r\n    MVCRp--\u003eEndpoints\r\n```\r\n\r\n**Two important things:**\r\n * Components doesn't have a reference to ASP.NET Core because it runs in other environments, and is what Razor Class Libraries target.\r\n * MVC and Razor Pages consume the SSR support for components.\r\n\r\nWith this in mind, information for the assets is exposed differently from StaticAssets and Components\r\n\r\n```mermaid\r\nflowchart TD\r\n    subgraph AspNet[ASP.NET Framework reference]\r\n        subgraph StaticAssets[Static Assets]\r\n            StaticAssetDescriptor\r\n            StaticAssetSelector\r\n            StaticAssetProperty\r\n            StaticAssetResponseHeader\r\n        end\r\n        Endpoints[Components Endpoints SSR]\r\n        MVCRp[Mvc and Razor Pages]\r\n    end\r\n    subgraph Components[Components]\r\n       ResourceAssetCollection\r\n       ResourceAsset\r\n       ResourceAssetProperty\r\n       ImportMapDefinition\r\n    end\r\n    ComponentsWasm[Components Webassembly]\r\n    ComponentsWebView[Components WebView]\r\n    ComponentsWasm--\u003eComponents\r\n    ComponentsWebView--\u003eComponents\r\n    Endpoints--\u003eComponents\r\n    Endpoints--\u003eStaticAssets\r\n    MVCRp--\u003eEndpoints\r\n```\r\n\r\n* ResourceAsset and its related types represent Blazor's view of a resource, which only includes things that are useful when including that resource in markup.\r\n* ResourceAssetDescriptor and its related types are the \"HTTP\" view of the file/endpoint that we mapped.\r\n\r\nThe Component endpoints assembly is the one responsible for mapping the `StaticAssetDescriptor`s into the `ResourceAssetCollection` so that Blazor and MVC can consume them.\r\n\r\n#### Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.dll\r\n\r\n```diff\r\nnamespace Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components;\r\n\r\npublic abstract class ComponentBase : IComponent, IHandleEvent, IHandleAfterRender\r\n{\r\n+    protected ResourceAssetCollection Assets { get; }\r\n}\r\n\r\npublic readonly struct RenderHandle\r\n{\r\n+    public ResourceAssetCollection Assets { get; }\r\n}\r\n\r\npublic abstract partial class Renderer : IDisposable, IAsyncDisposable\r\n{\r\n+    protected internal virtual ResourceAssetCollection Assets { get; } = ResourceAssetCollection.Empty;\r\n}\r\n\r\n+public class ResourceAssetCollection : IReadOnlyList\u003cResourceAsset\u003e\r\n+{\r\n+   public static readonly ResourceAssetCollection Empty = Is there an existing issue for this?\n\n- [x] I have searched the existing issues\n\n### Describe the bug\n\nAccording to the [documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/release-notes/aspnetcore-10.0?view=aspnetcore-10.0#client-side-fingerprinting), there appear to be two ways to enable client-side fingerprinting:\n\n1. Add the marker `#[.{fingerprint}]` to references so that non-framework static files are fingerprinted.\n2. Use the `StaticWebAssetFingerprintPattern` attribute to control which assets get fingerprinted.\n\nHowever, when I run dotnet publish for a Blazor WebAssembly app, the generated index.html automatically includes fingerprint markers for JavaScript files under wwwroot that are not part of the Blazor framework. The problem is that the actual file names are not rewritten to include the fingerprint. As a result, when hosting the contents of publish/wwwroot, those script requests return 404 errors because the referenced (fingerprinted) logical names do not exist on disk.\n\n```\nGET http://[::]:8000/lib/bootstrap/dist/js/bootstrap.bundle.min.493y06b0oq.js net::ERR_ABORTED 404 (File not found)\nGET http://[::]:8000/lib/bootstrap/dist/js/bootstrap.29cdq58tmq.js net::ERR_ABORTED 404 (File not found)\n```\n\n### Expected Behavior\n\nIf I do NOT configure any `StaticWebAssetFingerprintPattern`, non-framework JavaScript files should be referenced as-is (without fingerprint markers).\nAlternatively, if fingerprinting markers are added, the process should be consistent (either rewrite file names accordingly or avoid adding markers).\n\nThis appears aligned with the workaround mentioned in this issue comment:\nhttps://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/62211#issuecomment-3146544516\n\nIncluding the following in the project fixes the inconsistency:\n\n```xml\n\u003cStaticWebAssetFingerprintPattern Include=\"JS\" Pattern=\"*.js\" Expression=\"#[.{fingerprint}]!\" /\u003e\n```\n\nAdditionally, it is desirable for the template to work as is.\n\n### Steps To Reproduce\n\n1. Install .NET 10 RC2\n2. Run: dotnet new blazorwasm -f net10.0\n3. Run: dotnet publish\n4. Host the published app, e.g.:\n```\ncd bin/Release/net10.0/publish/wwwroot\npython3 -m http.server\n```\n5. Open the site in a browser and observe 404 errors for some JavaScript references.\n\n\n### Exceptions (if any)\n\n_No response_\n\n### .NET Version\n\n10.0.100-rc.2.25502.107\n\n### Anything Please describe the problem.\n\nApplications using `WebAssemblyHost` (e.g. Blazor WebAssembly clients) do not support hosted services out of the box. Services registered with `AddHostedService` are ignored when using `WebAssemblyHostBuilder`, unlike in applications built with `WebApplicationBuilder` or `HostApplicationBuilder`.\n\n### Describe the solution you'd like\n\n`WebAssemblyHost` should support automatically running hosted services registered with `AddHostedService`. \n\n### Additional context\n\nThis feature request has already been rejected in https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/33537. Background\r\n\r\nUpon initialization, the `dotnet watch` tool needs to know the set of available WebAssembly hot reload capabilities before the hot reload session starts. The current mechanism for this relies on the WebAssembly runtime having started up so it can be asked which capabilities it supports. However, in Blazor Web scenarios, WebAssembly runtime startup might be delayed indefinitely, which causes the mechanism to read hot reload capabilities to fail.\r\n\r\nWe worked around this problem in https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/pull/36195 by having a fallback, default set of capabilities to use if reading capabilities from the WebAssembly runtime fails.\r\n\r\n## Proposed solution\r\nWe could go one of two directions in the future to fully address this issue:\r\n* Expand the capabilities of `dotnet watch` to dynamically update the set of available capabilities if a new runtime becomes available (relatively high complexity)\r\n* Remove WebAssembly capabilities detection completely and rely on the fallback capabilities only (simpler)\r\n\r\nTo simplify the Blazor WebAssembly hot reload infrastructure and make the overall hot reload experience less error prone, I propose we go with the 2nd option that simplifies WebAssembly hot reload capabilities detection by having the full set of capabilities be known by the `dotnet watch` tool without having to dynamically fetch those capabilities from the WebAssembly Please describe the problem.\r\n\r\nIt's known issue that dotnet.wasm is a large file that every user of blazor browser should download. It's 44Mb for the project that I work on. Brotli compresses it to 9MB which is way better. However this compression comes at the cost that the client app needs to deal with the decompression by itself and needs brotly-dec-wasm library and each developer manually should mess around with the files and boot blazor.\r\n\r\n### Describe the solution you'd like\r\n\r\nIt'd be better if such job is done natively between server-browser. However there's a problem, that for instance, Azure CDN has a limit of 8MB for a file to be eligible for compressing. If it was possible to split dotnet.wasm during publishing to multiple chunks then this would problem resolved automatically on the browser level.\r\n\r\n### Additional context\r\n\r\nUPD 02.11.2023. Clarifying feature request a little bit here.\r\nThe way how Blazor publishes bundles does not play way with major CDN providers ([Azure](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cdn/cdn-improve-performance#azure-cdn-standard-from-microsoft-profiles) and [AWS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/ServingCompressedFiles.html) and [GCP](https://cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/dynamic-compression#response-not-compressed)) because they have limit ~10Mb for the file to be compressed. Blazor produces files within the bundle (dotnet.wasm specifically) which are larger than that thus making developers implement their own DIY loader if they want both consume compressed bundle and use those CDN providers.\r\nOne of ways to overcome this is to give developers the control of the maximum size of an item in the bundle. E.g. in ``.csproj`` file like:\r\n```\r\n\u003cMaxPublishItemSize\u003e5Mb\u003c/MaxPublishItemSize\u003e\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe metadata about file chunks can be reflected in ``blazor.boot.json`` file and used by the loaded to download and merge the chunks the fingerprinted endpoint if possible in addition to its regular path but do not fingerprint the actual file path on disk.\r\n    * This is because there are some files we don't have control of (like Currently, ASP.NET Core heavily relies on JavaScript for client-side operations, which can sometimes lead to performance bottlenecks, especially in complex web applications with intensive client-side processing. This reliance on JavaScript can limit the performance potential, particularly in scenarios requiring heavy computation or real-time data processing on the client side.\n\n### Describe the solution you'd like\n\nI propose the integration of WebAssembly (WASM) support within ASP.NET Core. This solution would involve:\r\n\r\nEnabling developers to write C# code that compiles to WebAssembly, allowing intensive computations to be run in the browser at near-native speeds.\r\nProviding seamless interoperability between WASM modules and existing JavaScript frameworks/libraries used in ASP.NET Core applications.\r\nOffering tools and documentation to assist developers in migrating performance-critical JavaScript code to C# (or another .NET language), which would then compile to WASM.\r\nEnsuring the WASM integration is aligned with the current development workflow in ASP.NET Core, allowing developers to adopt it incrementally in their existing projects.\r\nThe addition of WebAssembly support would significantly enhance the capabilities of ASP.NET Core for building high-performance, client-side web applications. providing both the runtime identifier and the `SelfContained` false flag to MSBuild (providing it via command line `--runtime` and either `--self-contained false` or `--no-self-contained` switches Files\\dotnet\\sdk\\7.0.100-rc.1.22431.12\\Sdks\\Microsoft.NET.ILLink.Tasks\\build\\Microsoft.NET.ILLink.targets(196,5): error NETSDK1102: Optimizing assemblies for size is not supported for the selected publish configuration. Please ensure that you are publishing a self-contained app. [*.Client.csproj]\r\n\r\nRelated previous issue: dotnet/aspnetcore#43068\r\n\r\nIn the pevious .NET release, providing the MSBuild flag /p:SelfContained=false (or modifying the project file) worked and produced a non-SCD build.\r\n\r\nWeirdly, the build DOES work if publishing via Visual Studio UI *or* when putting the `\u003cSelfContained\u003efalse\u003c/SelfContained\u003e` property in `Server.csproj`.\n\n### Expected Behavior\n\nPublishing via command line should work (for building via CI scenarios using the `dotnet` CLI).\r\n\r\nThe issue is probably related to how there needs to be two different builds for the Client project in this case: one self-contained and trimmed for the browser, and one possibly framework-dependent for the Server environment. WebPx.Sutz.Admin.Client\r\n\r\nMoved some files from Admin to Admin.Client to convert it to have all the required components for it to work as a PWA app also, like App.razor, Routes.razor, added an Index.html file, manifest.json, service-worker.js. Modified the Admin project to my layout on the client library as additional assemblies, with a little twist, AppLayout is a shared razor class library for allowing it to be on multiple clients.\r\n\r\n```\r\n    app.MapRazorComponents\u003cAppLayout\u003e()\r\n      .AddServerRenderMode()\r\n      .AddWebAssemblyRenderMode()\r\n      .AddAdditionalAssemblies(\r\n          typeof(WebPx.Components.Pages.Weather).Assembly\r\n      );\r\n```\r\n\r\nI know you currently don't have a Host model for the client (wasm) assembly in .net 8.\r\nI enabled some features on the Blazor Wasm Project:\r\n\r\n```\r\n\t\u003cStaticWebAssetBasePath\u003e/\u003c/StaticWebAssetBasePath\u003e\r\n\t\u003cServiceWorkerAssetsManifest\u003eservice-worker-assets.js\u003c/ServiceWorkerAssetsManifest\u003e\r\n\t\u003cBlazorCacheBootResources\u003efalse\u003c/BlazorCacheBootResources\u003e\r\n\t\u003cPublishTrimmed\u003etrue\u003c/PublishTrimmed\u003e\r\n\t\u003cBlazorEnableCompression\u003etrue\u003c/BlazorEnableCompression\u003e\r\n```\r\n\r\nAnd added the serviceworker.js support\r\n\r\n```\r\n\t\u003cItemGroup\u003e\r\n\t\t\u003cServiceWorker Include=\"wwwroot\\service-worker.js\" PublishedContent=\"wwwroot\\service-worker.published.js\" /\u003e\r\n\t\u003c/ItemGroup\u003e\r\n```\r\n\r\nSo the expected behavior is to load as server-side, service-worker would request all the assets and cache them in the browser, and serve the files from cache, but i'm currently not using the BlazorCacheBootResources because we end with multiple cache stores, one offline-cache-xxxx for each version of the service-worker-assets.js and one for the client. That's not optimal from the POV of client storage, leaving orphan files forever...
